A1.justification: Despite the changed title and substantial revision, both PDFs describe the same Hilbert-curve output representation. All main-text and appendix pages, including equations, tables and figures, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original ScanNet-based stereo experiments, quantization-error measurements, device profiling and supplementary mesh-reconstruction results.

after.justification: v2 reports original stereo and device experiments, plus KITTI evaluation and COCO human-pose experiments in Appendices C and F.

M1.justification: The stereo two-head architecture, Hilbert mapping and Hilbert penalty equations are retained. Appendix F introduces a training adaptation for pose estimation: train the original model first, then use its predictions as teacher targets for the modified model's Hilbert components.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates stereo depth using rendered ScanNet scenes. v2 adds outdoor training data from Virtual KITTI 2, evaluation on real KITTI 2012 images with sparse LiDAR ground truth, and COCO human-pose estimation using direct regression and heatmaps. These substantially extend the domains and tasks actually studied.

E2.justification: The depth comparisons retain the original DispNet and DPT models; KITTI extends the existing DispNet comparison. Appendix F adds comparisons against original ResNet-RS pose models with direct-regression and heatmap heads. The new precision variants are changes in evaluation settings.

E3.justification: The reported platform changes from SNPE 2.17 on Samsung S22/Snapdragon 8 Gen 1 to SNPE 2.24 on S24+/Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. v2 adds FP16 and W8A16 comparisons and replaces delta1 reporting with D1. Appendix C introduces a 194-image KITTI evaluation, 25/75 ScanNet–Virtual KITTI training mixture and different input/output resolutions.

E4.justification: v2 substantially revises the mechanism analysis through along-curve versus across-curve error distributions and pose-estimation success/failure cases. It also adds a coarse/fine coding failure discussion and a more complex depth example. v1's separate FP32 curve-order table and histograms disappear, while the mesh-fusion analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use scaled median absolute deviation to estimate quantization-error dispersion. Neither introduces independent repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance testing. v1's approximately five checkpoints concern model selection, not independent replications.

E6.justification: v2 adds precision/profiling, KITTI and pose results, including KITTI W8A8 D1 of 9.95% for DispNet versus 5.36% for h2DispNet. Existing scores also change: original DPT's DSP RMSE is 2.51 pixels in v1 Table 2 and 2.09 in v2 Table 1. These are revised results under changed reported hardware/settings, not established same-setting gains. Separate FP32 ablation results and delta1 entries are removed.

T1.justification: v1's Shannon–Hartley capacity/SNR argument is removed. v2 Section 2.4 substantially reformulates the error-reduction reasoning with explicit independence, error-magnitude and equal-dispersion assumptions. It separates the geometric bit-width increase from conditional quantization-error reduction, while retaining the principal mapping and loss equations.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a general quantization-improvement approach with approximately fivefold error reduction and less than 7% inference overhead. v2 makes high-precision depth from low-precision outputs the primary contribution, treats error reduction as conditional, and adds claims of W8A8 quality comparable to W8A16 with lower runtime and energy consumption.

C2.justification: v1 interprets Hilbert-component errors as independent. v2 identifies along-curve correlation and proposes that models may first learn the scalar quantity before converting it into Hilbert components, explaining failure to reduce error for direct pose regression. It also adds substantive limitations concerning retraining and integration into iterative depth-refinement architectures.

D1.justification: v2 adds pose-model and teacher-training details and changes the documented inverse LUT from 512×512 to 256×256. However, it omits v1's optimizers, learning-rate schedules, batch size, 150-pair calibration set, enhanced-quantizer option and checkpoint-selection description. These omissions materially reduce reproducibility information; they do not establish that those procedures changed.

R1.justification: The broad standalone discussion of QAT, PTQ and integer-only quantization is replaced by substantially different positioning within efficient depth prediction and hardware precision limits. v2 adds substantive comparisons with mixed-precision HDR processing and Jiang et al.'s quantized depth-completion approach, alongside modern depth architectures and pose-estimation literature.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusions are extensively rewritten around depth precision. Related work is integrated into the introduction, the method and experimental narrative are reorganized, a dedicated Discussion and Limitations section appears, and the supplementary material becomes an expanded, integrated appendix.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation, and the principal results table receives explicit precision/device columns. v2 adds an inference diagram, profiling and KITTI tables, and new diagnostic figures; expands the disparity illustration; and removes the LUT-map and separate FP32-analysis displays. Existing appendix mesh and depth figures are retained and reformatted.

improvement.justification: The correlation analysis and direct-regression failure case correct an important overgeneralization in v1's error-reduction explanation. Real-image KITTI evaluation and measured comparisons with W8A16 substantially strengthen evidence for applicability and deployment benefits. These gains outweigh the loss of training/calibration details, although reproducibility suffers and Section 3.4's latency/energy reduction percentages disagree with Table 2.
